c1bf7f8397ceede3f8fcbf48109ecfd52ab1e15d.message:
BACKENDS: EMSCRIPTEN: Bound the HTTP VFS chunk cache with LRU eviction

The range-request VFS caches downloaded chunks as files under /.cache in
MEMFS, i.e. on the wasm heap, and never freed them - a long session
streaming a large game (voice files alone can run to hundreds of MB) grew
the heap towards MAXIMUM_MEMORY and eventually OOMed the tab.

Add a session-wide LRU registry over the chunk files: every downloaded or
reused chunk is recorded, and once the total exceeds the cap (96 MB by
default, overridable in megabytes via the vfs_cache_limit config key, 0
disables) the least-recently-used chunk is unlinked. Chunks are only open
for the duration of a single read(), so eviction is always safe; if a
stream later touches an evicted chunk it clears its downloaded flag and
re-downloads transparently (one retry per chunk per read call). Full-file
downloads are not tracked: they only occur for files smaller than one
chunk or servers without range support, and could not be recovered
mid-stream.

Verified by booting IHNM (637 MB of data) with a 16 MB test cap: evictions
hold the cache at the cap, an evicted chunk was re-downloaded on demand,
and the game boots normally.

The range-request VFS caches downloaded chunks as files under /.cache in
MEMFS, i.e. on the wasm heap, and never freed them - a long session
streaming a large game (voice files alone can run to hundreds of MB) grew
the heap towards MAXIMUM_MEMORY and eventually OOMed the tab.

Add a session-wide LRU registry over the chunk files: every downloaded or
reused chunk is recorded, and once the total exceeds the cap (96 MB by
default, overridable in megabytes via the vfs_cache_limit config key, 0
disables) the least-recently-used chunk is unlinked. Chunks are only open
for the duration of a single read(), so eviction is always safe; if a
stream later touches an evicted chunk it clears its downloaded flag and
re-downloads transparently (one retry per chunk per read call). Full-file
downloads are not tracked: they only occur for files smaller than one
chunk or servers without range support, and could not be recovered
mid-stream.

Verified by booting IHNM (637 MB of data) with a 16 MB test cap: evictions
hold the cache at the cap, an evicted chunk was re-downloaded on demand,
and the game boots normally.

fa76b2197f44966dcd06a3c6211a710b2487b034.message:
BACKENDS: EMSCRIPTEN: Make the event recorder work on the web port

The event recorder (--enable-eventrecorder, a local/debug-only aid) never
worked on the Emscripten/SDL3 backend: it failed to compile, then crashed
at boot, then hung in-game while recording. Fix the whole chain, all rooted
in the recorder assuming an SDL timer manager that does not exist / does not
work under asyncify.

Compile:
- EventRecorder::getSurface() used SDL2's SDL_CreateRGBSurface() with the
  SDL_SWSURFACE flag, neither of which exists in SDL3. Use SDL_CreateSurface
  + SDL_GetPixelFormatForMasks() behind SDL_VERSION_ATLEAST(3,0,0), matching
  surfacesdl-graphics.cpp.
- OSystem_Emscripten::delayMillis() references g_eventRec without including
  gui/EventRecorder.h.

Boot crash ('null function'):
- OSystem_SDL::initBackend() unconditionally handed the recorder a new
  SdlTimerManager. SDL timers don't work in the Emscripten port (that is why
  EmscriptenTimerManager exists), so its callbacks trapped. Hand the recorder
  the platform's pre-created timer manager when one exists, and have
  EventRecorder::switchTimerManagers() recreate an EmscriptenTimerManager in
  passthrough mode under __EMSCRIPTEN__.
- OSystem_SDL::getTimerManager() returns the recorder's timer manager, which
  is null until initBackend(). The HTTP filesystem installs a timer during
  init() (before initBackend), so the first installTimerProc() dereferenced
  null. Fall back to the backend's own timer manager until the recorder has
  one; the handover adopts that same object so installed timers survive.
- delayMillis() pumps the recorder-owned timer manager via getTimerManager()
  and yields with SDL_Delay(0) when the recorder suppresses the real delay,
  since SDL_Delay is the asyncify suspend point and never yielding hangs the
  tab.

In-game record hang:
- ConnectionManager installs its polling timer proc on whatever TimerManager
  is active when the first request is queued and latches _timerStarted, so it
  is never reinstalled. Starting (or stopping) recording replaces the
  TimerManager, silently dropping that proc; on the web port the HTTP virtual
  filesystem drives its downloads from this timer, so in-game data loads hung
  forever (the download loop in http-readstream busy-waits on a request that
  is never processed). Add ConnectionManager::restartTimer() and call it from
  EventRecorder::switchTimerManagers() on Emscripten.

Recorder UI:
- Recordings live in the browser's virtual filesystem, which the user cannot
  reach directly. Add a Download button to the recorder dialog (guarded to
  Emscripten) that exports the selected recording via
  OSystem_Emscripten::exportFile(); it reuses the Delete slot in the theme
  layout and is repositioned in code to avoid regenerating the theme archives.
- Document the local --enable-eventrecorder build in build.sh.

Also suspend the recorder while the HTTP filesystem downloads game-data
chunks: the download busy-wait is wall-clock time unrelated to game logic,
so keep it out of the recorded timeline (same mechanism the GUI uses to
keep menus out of recordings).

4b51ac8a41e1c990d355e08733f5c1241b30c8a3.message:
BACKENDS: EMSCRIPTEN: Fix loading progress bar lagging behind byte counts

The fill's width was animated with a "width 0.5s ease" CSS transition
that got re-targeted on every downloaded chunk, while the "Downloaded
X / Y" text below it was written instantly with no transition. On a
fast connection the final, largest jump toward completion is still
mid-animation when the text already reports the download as finished,
so the bar visibly stalls at whatever width happened to be rendered
when the frame was captured (e.g. "Downloaded 33 MB / 33 MB" next to
an ~11% filled bar).

Drop the width transition entirely so the fill always snaps to the
same value backing the text. Also guard against unknown/zero totals
(missing Content-Length) which previously produced "NaN%"/"Infinity%"
widths that the browser silently ignored, and clamp the percentage to
100 to handle compressed transfers where decompressed bytes read can
exceed the reported Content-Length.

6bd21d3e9525cef479f026fcfda74fc2d123e6f5.message:
COMMON: Propagate finalize() through buffered and recorder write streams

BufferedWriteStream did not override finalize(), so the base implementation
only flushed its own buffer and never finalized the wrapped stream. When the
wrapped stream needs an explicit finalize to write trailing data - e.g. a
GZipWriteStream, which only emits its final deflate block and gzip trailer on
finalize - the output ended up truncated. The event recorder writes its
recordings through exactly this stack (buffered over compressed savefile), so
every recording came out as a truncated gzip archive that failed to parse on
playback. Flush the buffer, then finalize the parent.

PlaybackFile::updateHeader() likewise deleted its (compressed) write stream
without finalizing it; add the missing finalize() there too.

9517cd7b05194ec8b756f8505f80bdea49a3dd8f.message:
BACKENDS: EMSCRIPTEN: Keep the SDL audio callback out of the event recorder

The SDL3 audio callback runs from a WebAudio callback, usually while
Asyncify has the main loop suspended. It called g_system->getMillis()
to rate-limit a debug message. With the event recorder active, that
reaches EventRecorder::processMillis(), which updates the fake mixer and
runs every timer, and during playback also consumes the next recorded
event.

Running that from the audio callback can suspend again, for example
when a mixer update waits for HTTP game data. A nested suspend replaces
the suspended main stack's Asyncify data, so the next rewind traps. In
playback it also advances the replay from outside the main loop.

Use SDL_GetTicks() for the rate limit instead.
